column8: The consequences are concrete. When a theory can't tell you how to time your measurements or what shape a change process should take, you end up making design decisions based on convenience rather than substance. That's not a minor limitation — it means your study may be fundamentally mismatched to the phenomenon you're trying to understand.
column12: There's a persistent confusion in PD research between describing a phenomenon and explaining it. Laying out a diagnostic framework that organizes symptoms into dimensions is valuable, but it's not the same as having a theory about why someone develops enduring interpersonal dysfunction. We need to invest far more in the latter.
column16: This plays out very clearly in longitudinal research. If your theory doesn't specify how fast a process unfolds or what shape the trajectory should take, you can't derive a meaningful hypothesis about how many assessments you need or how far apart they should be. You end up designing studies based on budget and feasibility rather than on what the theory demands.
column24: When your key constructs are fuzzy, every downstream study inherits that fuzziness. Research designs that try to compare overlapping constructs end up generating ambiguous results, which then get interpreted through the lens of whichever framework the researcher already preferred. You can't build cumulative knowledge on a foundation of construct ambiguity.
column28: Tools and tutorials now exist that make formal modeling accessible to PD researchers without extensive computational backgrounds. The barrier at this point is more cultural than technical — the field simply hasn't prioritized this kind of work, and most researchers aren't trained in it.
column37: The issue isn't valuing methods too much — it's valuing them in the wrong way. Statistical power, model fit, and convergence criteria are important, but they can't substitute for the more fundamental question of whether your research design is actually matched to the process your theory describes.
column41: A diagnostic model that categorizes symptoms dimensionally is a step forward from categorical diagnosis, but it's still a measurement framework, not an explanatory theory. The field needs to be much clearer about this distinction and invest more in the genuinely explanatory work that goes beyond pattern description.
column57: If we want different research, we need different training. But beyond being "interesting", I don't know if radically abandoning old theories would actually be needed. For my field, I'd say we have many individualized derivatives of theories started in the 70ies, each fine tuned to a narrow range of applications, and in total actually "too many" theories rather than one single theory that would work well across domains.

column20: I've rarely seen a (previously considered plausible) theory abandoned based on empirical data. And I think this is a real problem. The nuance I'd add here is that models are often "fine-tuned" and applied only to a narrow range of tasks, while they predictably fail when applied to other tasks. In such situations, researchers often maintain that "it's still a good theory/model for the original task, and this other task needs another model; people might solve this other task using different mechanisms". So the domain of generalization for some theories/models seems to get narrower over time. And there seems little ambition to build models that actually generate behaviour for several tasks.
column24: My subfield is still quite "behaviorist" and many definition as operational, linked directly to observable behavioral patterns. But I can see how that's different in other fields (again those where it's intrinsically harder to "put numbers" on your stimulus material).
column28: In my field/the papers I read, > 90% of authors employ a computational model. It's also quite obviously incentived by journal editors to get papers sent out/published. But again, if your stimulus material (numbers, probabilities, economic values) is readily amendable to mathematical calculations, I feel that 90% of the hard work is already done. We know from applied statistics/economics how one *should* work with those numbers, so inspiration by normative models is high. Other phenomena are much harder to quantify, and I see much less plausibility in applying mathematical operations like multiplication or subtraction to phenomena like "feelings" or "stereotypes". I think it's just very hard. And I'm sceptical if it's a desirable/fair to expect similar models from other subfields of psychology.
column33: In my experience, every PhD student/postdoc has to master all skills 100% themselves, and there is no labour division on anything. But with the sharing of code and data, readily available summer schools, and more recently LLMs, people don't ask experts for help, they just (try to) do it themselves based on what's available on the internet. So I see this as a general trend of everyone becoming an "expert on everything" that is partly a consequence of knowledge becoming freely available on the internet.

column41: I hardly see people treat ANOVAs or linear regression models as "explanations", if that's the question. In some cases, I think those models do in fact embody different "mechanisms" of how "cognitive particles" might plausibly interact. But at other times, they seem to be mere "as if" models (e.g. when input variables are nonlinearly transformed and that's called a "perceptual distortion"). Hence, in my field, there are some models I have strong sympathy with, and others that are barely any different from linear regression, and I think the former are fine, but the latter actually harmful, and it's quite hard to argue with people about whether the boundary between those two lies.

column74: Regarding your purported link between theory development and the replication crisis: As long as effects are small and power low, you can have a theory that makes very precise predictions, but you're very unlikely to find empirical support for it. Under that scenario, I'm afraid it hardly makes any difference if you have a sophisticated or a shitty theory. This "high noise" problem needs to be fixed first. Only in a "high signal, low noise" scenario, the precision of theoretical predictions starts to matter.
